Intralobar pulmonary sequestration with.normalized_text: Intralobar pulmonary sequestration with superimposed infection
Intralobar pulmonary sequestration with.description: A congenital region of abnormal lung supplied by a systemic artery rather than the pulmonary circulation. The left posterobasal lesion and apparent vessel arising near the descending aorta favor pulmonary sequestration; infection can cause its first symptoms in childhood.

Extralobar pulmonary sequestration with.description: Congenital nonfunctioning lung tissue enclosed in its own pleural covering, usually near the lower lung and diaphragm, with systemic arterial supply. Infected congenital pulmonary airway mal.description: A congenital abnormality of distal airway development that may remain undetected until infection occurs. Hybrid lesions combine abnormal airway tissue with the systemic arterial supply characteristic of sequestration.

A 38-year-old woman presented with a three-day history of fever, generalized myalgia and arthralgia, and the sensation of difficulty when breathing in. She had poorly localized discomfort in the left diaphragmatic region on deep inspiration and loose stools over the preceding three days. Three days before presentation she had returned from a three-week trip to Western Australia, and 18 months earlier she had traveled to Vietnam. On examination she appeared well but was febrile at 38.0°C and tachypnoeic at 22 breaths/min, with all other observations normal. Examination of all other systems was unremarkable. Blood tests showed severe neutrophilia (18.9 × 10⁹/L; reference range 2.0-8.1), raised C reactive protein (354 mg/L; reference value <10), and normal renal and liver biochemistry. Chest radiography and urinalysis were normal. Blood cultures taken at presentation were negative.

Amoebic liver abscess.description: Hepatic infection caused by Entamoeba histolytica, sometimes presenting months or years after exposure in an endemic region. The apparent low-attenuation left hepatic lesion could represent an abscess, although imaging alone cannot establish its cause.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: A bacterial collection within the liver arising from biliary infection, portal spread, bloodstream infection, or an unidentified source. The apparent hepatic lesion and marked inflammatory response make this an important possibility.

Melioidosis with hepatic abscess.description: Infection with Burkholderia pseudomallei acquired from contaminated soil or water in endemic areas, including northern Australia and Southeast Asia. It can cause visceral abscesses and occasionally present after a prolonged latent period.

Pylephlebitis with secondary hepatic abs.description: Septic thrombosis of the portal venous system due to an intra-abdominal infection, potentially producing hepatic abscesses. The centrally indicated imaging abnormality warrants assessment of portal venous patency on the complete contrast-enhanced study.

Secondarily infected hepatic hydatid cys.description: An Echinococcus-related liver cyst complicated by bacterial infection, producing an abscess-like illness. This is a lower-probability alternative because characteristic cyst architecture is not clearly demonstrated in the supplied image.

She reported slow deterioration in vision from age 50, though she could still drive. Her mother was registered blind and had Parkinson's disease with dementia. On examination, she had a spastic gait with normal power in lower limbs but increased tone and sustained ankle clonus. Reflexes were brisk with flexor plantar responses. She had mild reduction in visual acuity and dyschromatopsia, but no detectable visual field defect and preserved pupillary light reflexes. CSF analysis showed presence of oligoclonal bands. Routine hematological, biochemical and immunological blood tests were normal, including folate and vitamin B12. Anti-aquaporin 4 antibodies were negative in serum.

Primary progressive multiple sclerosis.description: An inflammatory demyelinating disorder that can cause steadily progressive spinal cord dysfunction and optic nerve injury. OPA1-related dominant optic atrophy plus.normalized_text: OPA1-related dominant optic atrophy plus syndrome
OPA1-related dominant optic atrophy plus.description: An inherited mitochondrial disorder caused by OPA1 variants. In addition to bilateral optic atrophy, affected individuals can develop spasticity, peripheral neuropathy, ataxia and other neurological manifestations.

Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with a.normalized_text: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with an MS-like illness (Harding syndrome)
Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with a.description: A mitochondrial optic neuropathy associated with an inflammatory demyelinating syndrome resembling multiple sclerosis. Maternal transmission, optic atrophy and spinal cord symptoms can occur together.

Complicated hereditary spastic paraplegi.description: A group of inherited neurodegenerative disorders causing progressive corticospinal tract dysfunction together with additional features such as optic atrophy, neuropathy or cognitive changes.

Aquaporin-4-seronegative neuromyelitis o.description: An inflammatory disorder affecting the optic nerves and spinal cord that can occasionally occur without detectable aquaporin-4 antibodies. This presentation is less typical, and seronegative disease requires stringent clinical and MRI criteria.

Wilson disease with chronic hepatic invo.description: An autosomal recessive disorder of copper transport causing copper accumulation in the liver, brain, and cornea. Herbal medicine–induced liver injury, po.normalized_text: Herbal medicine–induced liver injury, potentially superimposed on Wilson disease
Herbal medicine–induced liver injury, po.description: Herbal preparations can cause hepatocellular, cholestatic, or mixed liver injury. Autoimmune hepatitis.description: Immune-mediated hepatic inflammation that can present in adolescent girls with chronic hepatitis, fibrosis, jaundice, and impaired hepatic synthetic function. Azathioprine-induced Sweet syndrome.description: A drug-triggered acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis causing painful red plaques or nodules and systemic inflammation. This is a leading possibility given the recent azathioprine exposure; skin biopsy is needed for confirmation.

Azathioprine hypersensitivity syndrome.description: An idiosyncratic systemic reaction, usually occurring within the first few weeks of azathioprine treatment, that can produce fever, rash, arthralgias, and marked inflammation. It can overlap with drug-induced Sweet syndrome.

Erythema nodosum.description: An inflammatory disorder of subcutaneous fat causing tender red nodules, usually on the shins, sometimes triggered by medications, infections, or systemic inflammatory disease.

Serum sickness-like reaction.description: A medication-associated inflammatory reaction characterized by fever, rash, and joint pain, often beginning one to two weeks after exposure. Unlike classic serum sickness, renal involvement is generally absent.

Drug-induced cutaneous small-vessel vasc.description: Inflammation of small dermal blood vessels triggered by medication or another immune stimulus, typically producing palpable purpura and sometimes fever or arthralgias. Skin biopsy distinguishes it from neutrophilic dermatoses.

Physical examination revealed visible neck swelling with bruising tracking onto the anterior chest wall. There was no tenderness on palpation of the cervical spine. On flexible nasal endoscopy, swelling of the posterior pharyngeal wall was observed, indicating potential airway compromise.

Traumatic retropharyngeal hematoma.description: Bleeding into the space behind the pharynx following neck trauma. This is the leading diagnosis given the marked prevertebral soft-tissue expansion on the supplied sagittal CT image and posterior pharyngeal swelling. An expanding hematoma can cause life-threatening airway obstruction.

Blunt laryngeal injury with associated h.normalized_text: Blunt laryngeal injury with associated hematoma
Blunt laryngeal injury with associated h.description: Traumatic injury to the laryngeal cartilage or soft tissues, producing edema, bleeding, and possible airway obstruction. Dedicated assessment is needed because the supplied image alone does not establish a laryngeal fracture.

Occult cervical ligamentous injury with.normalized_text: Occult cervical ligamentous injury with prevertebral hematoma
Occult cervical ligamentous injury with.description: A cervical ligament injury from the fall could cause bleeding and marked prevertebral swelling even without an obvious fracture. The absence of cervical spine tenderness does not exclude this injury.

Traumatic cervical vascular injury with.normalized_text: Traumatic cervical vascular injury with expanding neck hematoma
Traumatic cervical vascular injury with.description: Injury to a cervical vessel or branch can produce an enlarging hematoma that compresses the pharynx and airway. Vascular imaging would be needed to identify an active bleeding source.

case:
37-year-old man with 3 months of episodic weakness, irritability, poor concentration, craving sweets, foggy sensorium, cold clammy fatigue, and memory/behavioral changes, often occurring after several hours without food and worse at night or early morning. He gained 30 lb from drinking large amounts of cola for symptom relief. No significant medical history aside from prior umbilical hernia repair and back surgery; no medication use or diabetes diagnosis, though family history was positive for diabetes. On exam he was confused, cold, and clammy; other systems were unremarkable. Routine labs, HbA1c, and endocrine testing were largely normal except for mildly elevated prolactin. Imaging showed a 1.8 × 1.3 cm hypervascular slightly exophytic lesion at the anterior pancreas between the head and neck.

Pancreatic insulinoma.description: An insulin-secreting pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor, overwhelmingly the most likely diagnosis here. Glucose of 2.4 mmol/L with inappropriately elevated insulin and C-peptide and suppressed ketogenesis indicates endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia; the focal hypervascular pancreatic lesion strongly supports insulinoma.

Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 with.normalized_text: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 with pancreatic insulinoma
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 with.description: An inherited syndrome involving pancreatic neuroendocrine, pituitary, and parathyroid tumors. An insulinoma could explain the hypoglycemia, while prolactin elevation raises the possibility of pituitary involvement; mild prolactin elevation alone does not establish this syndrome.

Sulfonylurea- or meglitinide-induced hyp.description: Exposure to an insulin secretagogue can produce hypoglycemia with elevated endogenous insulin and C-peptide, closely mimicking insulinoma. A drug screen obtained during hypoglycemia helps distinguish this cause.

Adult non-insulinoma pancreatogenous hyp.description: Rare endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia caused by abnormal pancreatic beta-cell function, sometimes associated with diffuse nesidioblastosis, rather than a discrete insulin-secreting tumor.

Insulin autoimmune syndrome.description: A rare condition in which antibodies bind and subsequently release endogenous insulin, causing spontaneous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia. Insulin antibody testing can distinguish it from other causes.

Slipping rib syndrome.description: Hypermobility of the lower costal cartilages, usually ribs 8–10, causing intermittent subluxation and intercostal nerve irritation. This is the leading possibility. Intercostal or upper abdominal muscle st.normalized_text: Intercostal or upper abdominal muscle strain
Intercostal or upper abdominal muscle st.description: Overuse injury of the intercostal muscles or abdominal muscle attachments at the costal margin following repetitive loading.

Costochondritis.description: Inflammation or mechanical irritation of costochondral junctions causing movement-related anterior chest pain, generally involving the upper parasternal ribs.

Rib stress injury.description: Repetitive mechanical loading can produce a rib stress reaction or stress fracture without acute trauma. The supplied ultrasound images do not establish a fracture.

Colonic lymphangiomatosis.description: A rare benign lymphatic malformation producing multiple fluid-filled cystic lesions in the colonic wall, often covered by normal mucosa.

Colitis cystica profunda.description: A benign condition in which displaced colonic glands form mucin-filled cysts beneath the mucosa, sometimes creating polypoid or subepithelial lesions.

Myelodysplastic neoplasm with eosinophil.normalized_text: Myelodysplastic neoplasm with eosinophilia and associated eosinophilic lung disease
Myelodysplastic neoplasm with eosinophil.description: A clonal bone marrow disorder causing ineffective blood-cell production and abnormal cell maturation. This is a leading consideration given the anemia, dysplastic marrow morphology, eosinophilia, and apparent chromosome 1 and 7 abnormalities; definitive classification requires formal marrow and cytogenetic review.

Chronic eosinophilic leukemia.description: A clonal myeloid malignancy characterized by persistent eosinophilia and abnormal marrow findings, potentially causing eosinophil-mediated organ injury. Diagnosis requires molecular testing and exclusion of other defined myeloid neoplasms.

Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia.description: An eosinophilic inflammatory lung disease producing subacute or chronic respiratory symptoms, hypoxemia, and pulmonary consolidation. It can occur with asthma, but secondary causes of eosinophilia must be excluded.

Hypereosinophilic syndrome.description: A syndrome of substantial blood or tissue eosinophilia causing organ dysfunction. Pulmonary involvement can mimic asthma or eosinophilic pneumonia; this case particularly warrants evaluation for a clonal myeloid cause rather than an idiopathic syndrome.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyang.description: An eosinophil-rich systemic vasculitis associated with asthma and pulmonary infiltrates, sometimes accompanied by neuropathy, sinus disease, skin lesions, or kidney involvement. Negative ANCA testing does not exclude it.

His symptoms began with headache and abdominal pain, with an initial temperature of 38.6°C and pale skin. He experienced persistent upper abdominal pain and recurrent fevers. The patient reported nausea, occasional diarrhea, headache, myalgias, fatigue, and occasional dizziness. He described nearly constant periumbilical pain radiating to the left lower quadrant, with occasional blood in stools. His height was 132 cm (1st percentile), weight 26.8 kg (1st percentile), with recent 1 kg weight loss. Physical examination revealed pale skin and mucosa, distended abdomen with mild tenderness in right upper and left lower quadrants, and ecchymoses on the shins. He had visited the Dominican Republic 3 months prior. Laboratory tests showed severe microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 6.7 g/dL), elevated inflammatory markers (ESR >140 mm/hr, CRP 143.2 mg/liter), and elevated ferritin (320 μg/L).

Classical Hodgkin lymphoma.description: A lymphoid malignancy characterized by Hodgkin and Reed–Sternberg cells in an inflammatory background. This is the leading possibility given extensive metabolically active lymphadenopathy, a focal liver lesion, and apparent large atypical cells in the biopsy; definitive classification requires the labeled immunostains and pathology report.

Anaplastic large cell lymphoma.description: An aggressive T-cell lymphoma that can affect children and cause systemic inflammation, bulky lymphadenopathy, and extranodal lesions. It can resemble classical Hodgkin lymphoma, requiring immunophenotyping to distinguish them.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.description: An aggressive B-cell malignancy that may involve lymph nodes, bowel, and liver. Tissue architecture and B-cell immunostains are necessary for confirmation; the illustrated mixed inflammatory background is less typical than a diffuse proliferation of large malignant cells.

Disseminated tuberculosis with abdominal.description: A systemic mycobacterial infection that can produce prolonged fever, growth impairment, abdominal lymphadenopathy, and intestinal or hepatic lesions. It can mimic lymphoma on PET, but microbiologic testing and characteristic tissue findings are needed.

Crohn disease.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can cause abdominal pain, intestinal bleeding, iron-restricted anemia, and impaired childhood growth. It fits much of the clinical presentation but does not adequately explain the bulky multistation lymphadenopathy and atypical biopsy findings.

case:
A 39-year-old man presented to the emergency department during the summer with a 4-day history of fever with shaking chills, diffuse headache, and fatigue following his return from a 2-week trip to East Africa. During his trip to Tanzania, he had been on safari without animal contact but received mosquito bites, especially during the first days. He consumed cooked shrimp and lobster and a small amount of raw tuna. On the second-to-last day of the trip, he developed nausea, vomiting, and nonbloody diarrhea. Upon returning to Massachusetts, he experienced fever (38.3°C to 39.5°C), shaking chills, diffuse headache, and lower back pain. He reported weakness, anorexia, decreased urine output with dark urine, and blurry vision during fever episodes. His medical history included degenerative knee disease with previous glucocorticoid injections. On examination, he had a temperature of 38.9°C, blood pressure 113/62 mm Hg, facial flushing, mild scleral icterus, and dark brown urine.

Plasmodium falciparum malaria.description: Mosquito-transmitted parasitic infection of red blood cells and the leading diagnosis here. The malaria antigen test appears positive, and the blood smear shows numerous delicate intraerythrocytic ring forms, including double chromatin dots, strongly favoring falciparum malaria. Urgent assessment and treatment are required.

Babesiosis.description: An intraerythrocytic protozoal infection, usually transmitted by Ixodes ticks, that can cause fever, hemolysis, and thrombocytopenia. Massachusetts residence and ring forms make it a consideration, but the travel history and malaria antigen result favor malaria.

Dengue fever.description: A mosquito-borne viral infection occurring in East Africa that can cause acute fever, severe thrombocytopenia, and vascular leakage. It does not explain the demonstrated red-cell parasites.

Leptospirosis.description: A bacterial infection acquired through exposure to water or soil contaminated with infected animal urine. Severe disease can produce jaundice, kidney injury, and thrombocytopenia even without direct animal contact.

Hemolytic uremic syndrome.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy causing red-cell fragmentation, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury, sometimes following diarrheal illness. The demonstrated parasites instead strongly support malaria-associated hemolysis.

Delayed cervical esophageal or hypophary.description: Late erosion of cervical fixation plates or screws through the adjacent pharyngeal or esophageal wall can cause leakage and extensive infection. Descending mediastinitis with mediastina.description: A potentially life-threatening infection spreading from the neck or a pharyngoesophageal perforation into the mediastinum. The thoracic extent of the abscess and the image labels indicating mediastinal pus support this as a complication.

Retropharyngeal or prevertebral abscess.description: A deep neck-space infection that can produce painful swallowing and spread inferiorly along fascial planes. In this case, it may be secondary to hardware erosion or pharyngoesophageal perforation.

Delayed cervical spinal implant infectio.description: Infection involving spinal fixation hardware and potentially adjacent vertebrae can cause neck pain, fever, and paraspinal abscess formation. Vertebral involvement would require confirmation from detailed imaging or microbiologic evaluation.

Spontaneous pneumomediastinum from vomit.description: Vomiting can increase intrathoracic pressure enough to rupture alveoli, allowing air to track along bronchovascular structures into the mediastinum and neck. Esophageal perforation must first be excluded in this presentation.

Initial events involved shaking of the trunk and limbs lasting 4–5 minutes, preceded by occipital pain radiating to the neck, blurred vision, palpitations, nausea, and difficulty concentrating. Four months before admission, he had a stiffening episode with fall backward, generalized shaking for 5–8 minutes, and urinary incontinence. Despite levetiracetam, he continued to have seizures about weekly; one month before admission, he was found on the floor with shaking and clenching movements lasting about 2 minutes. On examination, he was awake and alert but nonverbal, with a stiff posture and intermittent nonrhythmic tremulous movements of the trunk and limbs. He had extensive burn scars on the face, trunk, back, arms, and legs. Past history included febrile seizure in childhood, several concussions, asthma, major depressive disorder, chronic PTSD, and panic disorder with agoraphobia. Labs were largely normal, with mildly elevated lactate and creatine kinase.

This is the leading possibility. The provided EEG appears to show prominent movement artifact with preserved posterior background activity rather than a clearly evolving ictal pattern; confirmation requires review of a typical episode on synchronized video-EEG.

Epilepsy with focal-to-bilateral tonic-c.description: An epileptic disorder in which seizures begin in a focal brain network and spread to produce bilateral stiffening and rhythmic jerking. It remains a differential diagnosis and can coexist with functional seizures, but the supplied EEG image does not establish an epileptic seizure.

Convulsive syncope.description: Transient reduction in cerebral blood flow, caused by a reflex faint or cardiac rhythm disturbance, can produce loss of consciousness accompanied by brief stiffening or jerking.

Panic attacks with dissociative symptoms.description: Episodes of acute autonomic arousal that can include trembling, impaired concentration, and altered responsiveness. Panic may contribute to or trigger functional seizures but does not by itself adequately explain every convulsive feature.

Incarcerated right obturator hernia caus.description: Small bowel becomes trapped in the obturator canal, particularly in thin, elderly, multiparous women. Incarcerated right femoral hernia causin.description: Bowel trapped in the femoral canal can cause acute obstruction and strangulation, especially in older women. Pelvic neoplasm causing small-bowel obst.description: A pelvic tumor can obstruct bowel and compress the obturator nerve, producing referred thigh or knee pain. This is substantially less likely because the provided CT images favor herniated bowel rather than a solid pelvic mass.

Two days later she developed sudden left-sided hearing loss. Three weeks after initial presentation, she reported right-eye visual field defect, and 2 days later was admitted for tinnitus, severe headache, and arm numbness. She denied diabetes, hypertension, connective tissue disease, tuberculosis, hematologic or cardiovascular disease, oral contraceptive use, and pregnancy. Exam showed reactive pupils without RAPD, corrected visual acuity 20/20 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye, normal intraocular pressure, and normal anterior segment findings. Laboratory tests were normal, including lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibody, ESR, and CRP. CSF showed mildly elevated protein (74.4 mg/dL) without oligoclonal bands; no specific hematologic or rheumatologic abnormalities were found.

Susac syndrome.description: The most likely diagnosis: an immune-mediated small-vessel endotheliopathy affecting the retina, cochlea, and brain, producing branch retinal artery occlusions, sensorineural hearing loss, and cerebral microinfarcts.

Multiple sclerosis.description: An inflammatory demyelinating disorder of the central nervous system that can cause relapsing visual and sensory disturbances and corpus callosum lesions.

Primary angiitis of the central nervous.normalized_text: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system
Primary angiitis of the central nervous.description: Inflammation of cerebral blood vessels causing headaches, focal neurologic deficits, and multifocal ischemic lesions, often without abnormal systemic inflammatory markers.

Antiphospholipid syndrome.description: An autoimmune thrombophilia that can cause retinal arterial occlusions and cerebral ischemic events; cochlear ischemia is a less common manifestation.

Atypical Cogan syndrome.description: An inflammatory oculo-audiovestibular disorder involving sensorineural hearing loss and ocular inflammation; atypical forms can include retinal vasculitis and systemic vascular disease.

Ileal leiomyosarcoma.description: A malignant smooth-muscle tumor that can arise in the intestinal wall and cause bleeding. It is a histologic differential diagnosis, but the reported KIT mutation strongly favors GIST instead.

Ileal neuroendocrine tumor.description: A neoplasm of intestinal neuroendocrine cells that commonly arises in the distal ileum and may appear as an enhancing mass. This is an imaging differential, but the molecular findings strongly argue against it.

Gastric gastrointestinal stromal tumor.description: A gastrointestinal mesenchymal neoplasm that commonly arises in the stomach and may grow outward into a large mass with hemorrhage and necrosis. Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pa.description: A pancreatic neoplasm of low malignant potential that can become large and develop extensive hemorrhagic degeneration. Solid areas and cells arranged around delicate vessels can create a pseudopapillary appearance.

Nonfunctioning pancreatic neuroendocrine.description: A pancreatic endocrine-cell neoplasm without a clinically evident hormone-excess syndrome. Such tumors may present as large masses, with nested or trabecular histology and a prominent vascular network.

Gastric schwannoma.description: A usually benign nerve-sheath tumor of the gastric wall that can produce an outward-growing mass. Diagnosis typically requires spindle-cell morphology, a peripheral lymphoid cuff, and S100 or SOX10 expression.

Darier disease.description: An inherited disorder of keratinization and cell adhesion that produces crusted keratotic papules, sometimes with prominent flexural involvement. Histology typically shows acantholysis with conspicuous dyskeratosis rather than the extensive acantholysis suggested here.

Pemphigus vegetans.description: A rare autoimmune pemphigus variant producing blistering followed by thickened, vegetating plaques, particularly in intertriginous areas. Confirmation requires compatible histology and immunofluorescence.

Chronic candidal intertrigo.description: Inflammation of moist skin folds complicated by Candida overgrowth. It could contribute secondary infection but would not adequately explain the apparent acantholytic biopsy findings.

Giant cell tumor of bone with secondary.description: A locally aggressive bone tumor in skeletally mature young adults that can produce marked bone expansion and secondary hemorrhagic cystic changes. Pelvic involvement is uncommon but possible.

Chondromyxoid fibroma of the left ilium.description: A rare benign cartilage-forming tumor that generally affects young adults and may appear as an expansile, lobulated lytic lesion. Iliac lesions can become large and mimic malignant tumors.

Chondroblastoma with secondary aneurysma.description: A rare benign cartilage-producing tumor, usually arising near the end of a bone in adolescents or young adults. Secondary aneurysmal bone cyst formation can cause substantial expansion.

Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.normalized_text: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus
Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.description: A severe stiff-person-spectrum disorder, frequently associated with glycine-receptor antibodies, that causes rigidity, spasms, exaggerated reflexes, and often brainstem or autonomic dysfunction. Inflammatory myelopathy.description: Immune-mediated spinal cord disease can produce progressive spastic paraparesis, painful spasms, hyperreflexia, and clonus. Spinal MRI and assessment for sensory and sphincter abnormalities would help distinguish it from stiff-person syndrome.

Severe atherosclerotic supra-aortic occl.description: Advanced narrowing or occlusion of arteries supplying the brain and scalp can cause cerebral hypoperfusion and, rarely, ischemic scalp ulceration and hair loss. Takayasu arteritis.description: A large-vessel vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, especially in younger women. Severe branch-vessel stenosis can produce cerebral and peripheral tissue ischemia.

Giant cell arteritis with scalp necrosis.normalized_text: Giant cell arteritis with scalp necrosis
Giant cell arteritis with scalp necrosis.description: An inflammatory disease of medium and large arteries that can compromise scalp perfusion and cause ulceration or necrosis. It is exceptionally uncommon before age 50.

Pressure-induced ischemic alopecia with.normalized_text: Pressure-induced ischemic alopecia with scalp ulceration
Pressure-induced ischemic alopecia with.description: Prolonged pressure on the scalp can impair local circulation, causing focal hair loss and, in severe cases, skin necrosis. This usually follows prolonged surgery or immobilization, neither of which is established in the provided history.

Labs then showed anemia, leukopenia with neutropenia, hypergammaglobulinemia, high rheumatoid factor, positive ANA, low C4, positive anti-dsDNA, and cryoglobulins; HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C tests were negative. On admission, she had fever and pancytopenia, without hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Blood film, cultures, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, CMV PCR, and tuberculin test were negative. Visceral leishmaniasis with secondary cr.description: The leading diagnosis is disseminated Leishmania infection, likely L. infantum acquired through sandfly exposure in Greece, with dogs serving as reservoirs. Anti-TNF therapy increases susceptibility. The microscopy shows numerous small organisms consistent with Leishmania amastigotes, and the serum image supports cryoprecipitation. Adalimumab-induced lupus-like syndrome.description: TNF inhibitor therapy can induce a lupus-like autoimmune syndrome with arthritis, fever, skin manifestations, ANA, and anti-dsDNA antibodies. It is an important alternative but does not explain the apparent organisms on microscopy.

Systemic lupus erythematosus with immune.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with immune-complex vasculitis
Systemic lupus erythematosus with immune.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that can cause inflammatory arthritis, cytopenias, complement consumption, and vasculitic skin lesions. Infection-induced autoantibodies and anti-TNF exposure complicate interpretation of the lupus serology.

Mixed cryoglobulinemic vasculitis.description: Cryoglobulin-containing immune complexes cause small-vessel inflammation, commonly with purpura, arthralgia, high rheumatoid factor, and low C4. Here it likely represents a secondary manifestation of infection rather than an independent explanation for the entire illness.

Felty syndrome.description: A complication of rheumatoid arthritis characterized by neutropenia, usually with splenomegaly, and susceptibility to infection. It could explain some hematologic findings but is a substantially weaker fit than visceral leishmaniasis.

Granuloma annulare.description: A benign granulomatous skin condition typically causing annular plaques composed of firm papules. Histology generally shows focal collagen degeneration surrounded by histiocytes and increased dermal mucin.

Diabetic dermopathy.description: A diabetes-associated skin condition producing small, brown, mildly atrophic pretibial spots, usually multiple and asymptomatic.

Morphea.description: Localized scleroderma causes slowly evolving inflammatory plaques that become sclerotic, discolored, and sometimes centrally depressed. Histology typically demonstrates thickened, densely packed dermal collagen.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B due to.description: The most strongly supported diagnosis. Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A.description: A disorder usually caused by a maternally inherited inactivating GNAS coding variant, resulting in resistance to parathyroid hormone and other hormones. Post-traumatic phagophobia.description: An intense fear of swallowing after a frightening choking event, potentially leading to severe food avoidance and dehydration. It could contribute to this presentation but cannot explain the biochemical and methylation abnormalities.

Esophageal food bolus impaction.description: Retention of swallowed food in the esophagus can cause acute dysphagia, drooling, regurgitation, and inability to tolerate food or liquids. The initial choking episode makes this a consideration, although it does not explain the broader findings.

Dabrafenib–trametinib-associated severe.normalized_text: Dabrafenib–trametinib-associated severe pyrexia syndrome with drug-induced liver injury
Dabrafenib–trametinib-associated severe.description: Combined BRAF and MEK inhibition frequently causes fever and can produce a severe systemic reaction with hypotension, dehydration, kidney injury, and hepatic inflammation.

Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.description: A potentially life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome triggered by infection, malignancy, or medication. Ferritin, triglycerides, soluble interleukin-2 receptor levels, and additional clinical criteria are needed to assess this possibility.

Bacterial sepsis with disseminated intra.description: A systemic bacterial infection can cause circulatory instability, organ injury, and consumptive coagulopathy; an abdominal or pulmonary source would require investigation.

Human monocytic ehrlichiosis.description: A tick-borne Ehrlichia infection that can cause fever, cytopenias, hepatitis, and, in severe cases, shock, coagulopathy, and respiratory or renal dysfunction.

Primary pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.description: A primary pancreatic malignancy that can cause pancreatic duct obstruction, pancreatitis, and biliary obstruction. Tissue immunophenotyping is needed to distinguish it from metastatic prostate cancer.

Acute cholecystitis.description: Inflammation of the gallbladder, usually caused by cystic duct obstruction from a stone, but occasionally associated with malignant obstruction. It could explain the later presentation while coexisting with pancreatic malignancy.

Acute biliary pancreatitis from transien.normalized_text: Acute biliary pancreatitis from transient choledocholithiasis
Acute biliary pancreatitis from transien.description: Pancreatic inflammation caused by a gallstone transiently obstructing the ampulla. A passed stone may leave normal bilirubin and subsequently normal lipase.

Distal cholangiocarcinoma.description: A malignancy of the distal common bile duct that may resemble a pancreatic head mass and impair biliary or pancreatic drainage. It is less favored without demonstrated bile duct origin or supportive immunophenotyping.

X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.description: An ABCD1-related disorder of very-long-chain fatty acid metabolism that can cause childhood adrenal insufficiency and progressive cerebral or spinal neurologic disease in boys.

Familial glucocorticoid deficiency.description: A genetically heterogeneous disorder of adrenal ACTH responsiveness or steroid production causing cortisol deficiency with relatively preserved aldosterone secretion. GMPPA-related alacrima-achalasia-intelle.description: An autosomal recessive glycosylation-related disorder producing alacrima, achalasia, developmental impairment, and sometimes autonomic abnormalities. It resembles Allgrove syndrome but typically lacks adrenal insufficiency.

Multifocal cerebral infarction from mali.normalized_text: Multifocal cerebral infarction from malignancy-associated hypercoagulability or nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis
Multifocal cerebral infarction from mali.description: Advanced cancer can cause thrombosis or sterile cardiac valve vegetations that embolize to multiple cerebral territories. Cerebral venous thrombosis with hemorrha.normalized_text: Cerebral venous thrombosis with hemorrhagic venous infarction
Cerebral venous thrombosis with hemorrha.description: Thrombosis of cerebral veins or dural sinuses can produce cortical and subcortical edema, hemorrhage, and encephalopathy. Cancer increases the risk; MR or CT venography is needed to assess this possibility.

Intracranial metastatic breast cancer, i.normalized_text: Intracranial metastatic breast cancer, including leptomeningeal metastasis
Intracranial metastatic breast cancer, i.description: Breast carcinoma can spread to brain tissue or leptomeninges, causing cognitive decline, weakness, and altered consciousness. Toxic-metabolic encephalopathy, includin.normalized_text: Toxic-metabolic encephalopathy, including hepatic encephalopathy or hypercalcemia of malignancy
Toxic-metabolic encephalopathy, includin.description: Liver dysfunction, elevated calcium from malignancy, or other metabolic disturbances can cause generalized weakness and rapidly progressive encephalopathy. These possibilities require laboratory assessment and could coexist with a structural brain process.

Intramedullary spinal tuberculoma.description: A focal granulomatous tuberculosis infection within the spinal cord can produce an enhancing lesion and progressive myelopathy. Tissue microbiology and assessment for caseating necrosis are needed to distinguish it from sarcoidosis.

Fungal granulomatous myelitis.description: Rare fungal infections can cause granulomatous spinal cord lesions resembling neurosarcoidosis. Identification requires appropriate tissue stains, cultures, or molecular testing; the supplied images alone do not establish an organism.

Inflammatory demyelinating cervical myel.description: An inflammatory demyelinating spinal cord disorder, including idiopathic transverse myelitis, can cause subacute motor, sensory, and autonomic dysfunction. The apparent granulomatous biopsy findings make this less likely than neurosarcoidosis.

Intramedullary spinal cord neoplasm.description: A cervical intramedullary tumor, such as an ependymoma or astrocytoma, can cause progressive asymmetric myelopathy. It is an imaging differential, but the supplied biopsy appearance favors granulomatous inflammation rather than a tumor.

Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia with lun.normalized_text: Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia with lung abscess formation
Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia with lun.description: A bacterial lung infection causing tissue destruction and cavities within consolidation, sometimes following a viral respiratory illness. Microbiologic testing is necessary to establish the organism.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can produce persistent cough, cavitary pulmonary lesions, and granulomatous inflammation. Confirmation requires respiratory molecular testing and mycobacterial cultures, with tissue stains when appropriate.

Pulmonary actinomycosis.description: A relatively uncommon bacterial infection, usually associated with aspiration of oral organisms, that can cause peripheral consolidation, abscesses, and extension toward the pleura. Pulmonary blastomycosis.description: An environmentally acquired fungal infection that can cause pneumonia-like consolidation, nodules, cavitation, and suppurative granulomatous inflammation. Corticobasal degeneration presenting as.description: A neurodegenerative tauopathy usually associated with asymmetric rigidity, apraxia, and cortical dysfunction. Spinocerebellar ataxia type 2.description: An inherited neurodegenerative disorder that can cause progressive ataxia, markedly slow saccades, ophthalmoplegia, and sometimes parkinsonism. Genetic testing would be needed for confirmation.

Adult-onset Niemann-Pick disease type C.description: A rare inherited intracellular lipid-trafficking disorder that can cause vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, ataxia, dystonia, and progressive swallowing impairment. Presentation at this age would be unusual.

A 36-year-old man, sexually active with men, presented to the emergency department with a 2-week history of fever, headache, drowsiness, and photophobia. He was previously healthy. Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein anti.description: An antibody-associated inflammatory demyelinating disease that can cause longitudinally extensive, centrally located spinal cord lesions in children and adolescents. Confirmation requires compatible clinical findings and serum MOG-IgG testing.

Aquaporin-4 antibody-associated neuromye.normalized_text: Aquaporin-4 antibody-associated neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder
Aquaporin-4 antibody-associated neuromye.description: An autoimmune astrocytopathy that can present with longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, sometimes before optic neuritis develops. Spinal cord infarction.description: Ischemic injury of the spinal cord, occasionally caused by fibrocartilaginous embolism in young patients. Acute spinal pain, weakness, and loss of pain or temperature sensation may occur; diffusion-weighted MRI and the timing of symptom progression are important discriminators.

Syringomyelia or symptomatic hydromyelia.description: A fluid-filled cavity or dilated central canal within the spinal cord that can impair crossing temperature-sensation pathways and motor tracts. The thin central signal visible on the supplied sagittal images raises this structural alternative, but axial sequences and assessment of fluid-equivalent signal are needed.

T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia.description: An aggressive mature T-cell leukemia usually affecting older adults. Its mature T-cell immunophenotype can resemble TdT-negative T-ALL; confirmation generally requires appropriate morphology and TCL1-family abnormalities or expression.

Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by uncontrolled immune activation, often triggered by infection or malignancy. Disseminated tuberculosis with secondary.description: Systemic Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can involve the lungs and other organs and trigger HLH. Disseminated fungal infection with secon.normalized_text: Disseminated fungal infection with secondary HLH
Disseminated fungal infection with secon.description: Systemic fungal infections, including histoplasmosis or talaromycosis where epidemiologically relevant, can involve the lungs and reticuloendothelial system and provoke HLH. Lymphoma-associated HLH.description: An occult lymphoma, particularly a T-cell or NK-cell lymphoma, can trigger severe systemic immune activation and HLH even without a prior malignancy diagnosis.

Severe multifocal pneumonia with sepsis,.description: A severe pulmonary infection can cause systemic circulatory dysfunction, diffuse inflammatory lung injury, cytopenias, and coagulation abnormalities. It may coexist with or trigger HLH.

Dengue virus encephalitis.description: A neurologic manifestation of mosquito-borne dengue infection that can produce direct brain inflammation, occasionally with focal deficits or vascular complications.

Varicella-zoster virus meningoencephalit.normalized_text: Varicella-zoster virus meningoencephalitis with cerebral vasculopathy
Varicella-zoster virus meningoencephalit.description: Varicella-zoster virus can inflame cerebral arteries and cause multifocal ischemic injury, sometimes without a preceding shingles eruption. Advanced age increases susceptibility.

West Nile virus neuroinvasive disease.description: A mosquito-borne infection that can cause encephalitis, coma, and asymmetric weakness, with especially severe disease in older adults.

Acute bacterial meningoencephalitis with.description: Bacterial infection of the meninges and brain can cause coma and inflammatory arterial injury with focal ischemic deficits. It remains an urgent exclusion in a febrile comatose patient.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.description: A necrotizing vasculitis that can affect the upper airways, lungs, kidneys, skin, and joints. Chronic follicular cystitis with reactiv.description: A benign inflammatory response to recurrent bladder irritation or infection that produces prominent lymphoid aggregates and can mimic lymphoma.

Rectal leiomyosarcoma.description: A malignant smooth-muscle tumor that can arise within the rectal wall and produce a bulky spindle-cell mass. Diagnosis requires assessment of atypia, mitoses, necrosis, and smooth-muscle immunostains.
